title: I’m building an extraction deckbuilder solo with AI. Would you want to try it?
author: Verciau
selftext:
[I’m building DEEPWELL solo with AI: a deckbuilding roguelite with extraction risk.](https://reddit.com/link/1wziroj/video/e1x7iijapxth1/player)

I’m building DEEPWELL solo, with AI helping me work through the code and iterate on the game. There’s a lot of back and forth.

DEEPWELL is my attempt to mix the deckbuilding roguelite runs I love in Slay the Spire and Across the Obelisk with the extraction risk of ARC Raiders and Escape from Tarkov. You build a collection of cards and choose what to bring into a dive. From there, you decide whether to get out with what you’ve found or push further and risk losing what you brought and what you looted along the way.

Plenty of other roguelites have inspired me too. I’ve wanted to share a game of my own for years.

Building with AI took a lot of testing and retesting. I started with Claude Fable 5.1, then used Codex 5.6 Sol for gauntlet loops and image generation. Thank goodness gpt-image-2.5 gave me transparent backgrounds. That saved a TON of cleanup.

Then I had 300+ cards and five times as many concepts to sort through. Codex built me a review site that was basically a dating app for card art: pick the better one, then do it again. And again, until there were clear winners.

I matched each card’s theme, HERO, and art, tried sampled audio cues for several cards, and experimented with special faces and video-generated card animations.

It was long and tedious, especially getting the cards to work and feel right across devices. But I ended up with distinct deck options and different ways to dive into DEEPWELL. There’s more to refine, but getting those core deck ideas together was a big goal of mine.

6 Astra burned through my weekly allowance, and development slowed. With my tokens on fumes, I tried other models in OpenCode, my favorite agent. Opus 5.5 won me over as I worked through UI screens, the options menu, performance, cloud reliability, player save backups, 3D assets, and more.

For the game itself, I chose human-made music from open-source music libraries. I really liked this music I found, it had a very nice vibe I wanted and felt compelled to keep it.

I made this video with AI to promote my game. The narration is an AI clone of my own voice, and the music in this particular video is generated too. All with ElevenLabs and Opus 5.5

I’m planning to release DEEPWELL on web, Mac, Windows, Steam, and iOS. I also have a working multiplayer mode.

Anyways, there’s plenty more I could share, but for now I’m just looking for a temperature check. Does mixing deckbuilding with extraction risk sound fun to you? What would put you off trying it?

If you’d like to follow along: [playdeepwell.com](https://playdeepwell.com/) · [X](https://x.com/deepwellgame) · [TikTok](https://www.tiktok.com/@deepwellgame) · [Discord](https://discord.gg/kYBCDHnGsD).

comments.author: AsparagusOk8818
comments.body:
I sincerely wish you much more luck than I had, taking a crack at this concept. I ended up abandoning it in prototyping because I just couldn't find the fun.

Here are the problems I ran into - not posted as discouragement, but just to share the lessons I learned while trying at this idea: 

 \- There is a lot of inherent friction between the idea of an extraction-style game and a roguelike. They SEEM like they ought to complement each other... but they fight each other, a lot. A substantial problem is what the end of a run should look like; in an extraction-style game, you want to leave with more than what you came in with. The whole point of a Tarkov mission is that you're being careful with sparse resources and then, hopefully, picking up a few more. In a roguelike, by the end of a run you're supposed to have some kind of absurd engine online, at least in a good run. You're supposed to pop-off and then reset, because if you could keep the pop-off deck the game would stop working.

How are you supposed to blend these things together? The rogulike wants you to reset, the extraction game wants you to acquire. I personally couldn't find a satisfying way to merge the concepts (there ARE answers, but none of them seemed like fun to me).

 \- Snowballing is a huge issue. A Roguelike wants the player to be able to snowball - a lot of the fun in a good roguelike is the contrast between a trash run and a God run and every experience in between those things. Snowballing is how that difference in experience even happens, most of the time. Extraction games, by contrast, deliver fun by offering a very shallow and careful gradient of power. You can really feel each incremental advantage you get in Tarkov, and that's the thrill of it. That's why it feels so amazing to get out with a nice haul, and why it feels so devastating to lose it, and how that translates into the kind of tension that causes players to be nervous about firefights and negotiate with each other. 

If you snowball, you lose the gentle power gradient. If you keep the gentle power gradient, the roguelike runs feel too flat and samey - they stop feeling like runs and start feeling like grinds. I could not figure out any solution for this problem.

 \- Extraction games require opposition that you can negotiate with. It's a fundamental part of the payoff for the tension. This is fully possible in a single player roguelike game... but, IMHO, it is never very satisfying. Eventually the player will know the optimal dialogue routing or optimal other negotiating strategy and it no longer feels like a meaningful interaction.

It also conflicts with a fundamental payoff for roguelike experiences - speed. Roguelike runs are supposed to be quick and punchy. Extraction games are slow, methodical... at times, providing this weird sense of gritty, gruelling emotion that few other games explore in a good way. Negotiation hooks into that emotion at a core level.

again, I couldn't figure out how to get these elements to work in harmony with each other. In all of my prototyping, they constantly fought and produced - at best - mediocre gameplay.

  
I hope that's useful food for thought and can find creative ways to get around those problems that I couldn't.

Good luck!

replies.author: hawtdawtz
replies.body: People pay money for this type of advice. Very well said and be applied in so many ways outside of this example.

replies.author: Verciau
replies.body:
Thanks for taking the time to share this. I appreciate hearing what you ran into trying it yourself.

I agree on some level. Finding the fun is a never-ending mission when you’re carving out new ideas, and I’m still figuring it out.

In DEEPWELL, you keep base copies of cards while the upgrades and relic combos reset after each dive. That’s my starting point for making the two ideas work together.

Snowballing is probably the hardest part. Extracting needs to feel good even when you’ve built a deck you want to keep playing. I don’t have that all solved yet.

I’m hoping choosing what to risk and when to leave can create enough tension on its own. Your points give me a lot to watch for as I keep testing! Thank you 🙏

replies.author: Smok3dSalmon
replies.body:
Pretty interesting tension that you described. KCD2 has an interesting negative perk system in hardcore mode. Perhaps you could do have a system where you are willingly taking on negative perks in order to increase your extraction rewards or to unlock positive perks. 

Enter with a broken leg, but you double your luck.

But this might be a departure from the original idea

replies.author: Verciau
replies.body:
I love this. The balance is between feeling powerful going into a custom dive with your preferred cards, and feeling challenged enough that you start to calculate how far you can go and where to make your exit. 

Regular players will become familiar with this as they discover and learn the creatures of Deepwell and their actions.

replies.author: Smok3dSalmon
replies.body:
You should see the KCD2 negative perks, there is a hilarious one called “Sleep Walking” when you sleep there is s chance that your character sleep walks and you’ll wake up somewhere new. You also get no map on hardcore mode.

replies.body: Your negative perks could involve reducing the size of the players deck. Maybe a perk like “One Trick” where you only get 1 card but you can play it over and over

comments.author: i_am_the_baffler
comments.body: I'm interested!  Looks cool.  What tech/language/framework(s) did you use to build the game?

replies.author: Verciau
replies.body: Thanks! Typescript with ThreeJS is a big piece but Swift for some native iOS capabilities. I use Astra for design and animation based work, Sol for everything else, Opus 5.5 to validate and loop fixes/improvements using p-stack clones or similar “harnesses” to keep things efficient (aka stop wasting my tokens on slop).
